Question: What are the weirdest things flight attendants have seen in their line of duty?
Answer: Well the weirdest/scariest thing I've witnessed on board an aircraft was having a near death experience on a single aisle aircraft. I'm seated on the right side of the cabin facing passengers and it's a normal 45 mins flight. Around 50-60 seconds after take off suddenly the aircraft tips to its left...hard left..so much so that I realised my hands quickly moving to grab my 4 point harness over my chest to prevent myself from hanging weirdly from my jump seat. Everything after that moment was like a slow motion movie. I remember having a quick glance at my crew seated on the adjacent door and I saw her eyes wide open and almost gasping for breath and simultaneously pushing her body away from the door as she was almost falling off on to it due to gravity. I heard someone in particular scream, a guy voice, "oh Lord!!" and in a fraction of a second I had these pictures of my family and friends and even my ex-gfs flash in front of my eyes like a continuous flow of a powerpoint presentation. As the aircraft had banked to its extreme left and literally its left wing pointing straight towards the sea we were flying on I could see a few unsecured loose objects falling off towards the left of the fuselage and colliding with seat's head rest before falling on the left side. In particular I remember seeing something that I believe was an i-pad falling off and started rotating at a crazy speed after hitting one of its edge on the headrest and thumping on one of the windows. All this happened within a short span of 4-5 seconds before the aircraft started aligning to a rather normal position. After a good 5 mins the captain gave us the signal by switching the seatbelt sign off n on that it was safe for Crew to move for the snacks service but my legs felt weak and were trembling until we landed. Later we learned from the captain that he was forced to take that maneuver in order to avoid getting into a mid-air collision path with a double deck AIRBUS 380. As ours was a way smaller aircraft it was easier for it to have had made that maneuver faster compared to the A-380. We didn't bother to ask how it was possible, was it the ATC's fault or the A-380's or what went wrong as we were just thankful to be alive that day and grateful to the flightdeck crew's decision. Myself and the crew did not see even 1 passenger on that flight went to use the washroom. Snacks were barely and I mean barely consumed that day. Part and parcel of crew life.

Question: What are the different qualities of a cabin crew?
Answer: First and foremost is being able to remain calm and composed to assess a situation and act accordingly. It can be anything from handling a very demanding passenger to a medical case on-board or even preparing the passengers for a crash landing. Also being vigilant and knowing what's not normal is important. Once during service our aircraft was flying over the ocean and quite suddenly I realised a very unusual vibration throughout the fuselage causing weird creeking noises, immediately i called up flight deck and it turned out the Pilot-in-command (PIC) had given full control to one of the trainee pilot who was increasing the altitude of the aircraft at an incredible speed and that too at quite a steep angle thus increasing the drag and causing the vibrations. Cabin crew are the eyes and ears and nose of the flight deck, anything we see hear or smell that is unusual we need to inform the PIC. Thinking of the top of your head and being able to act quickly is another trait that's very much needed in this job. Incase of a medical emergency when your colleague needs you to get a medical kit, oxygen and help, you really have to be fast as every passing second is important. And of course being able to smile at all points of customer interaction is a great deal for the hiring airlines.

Question: What is the difference between check in and cabin bag?
Answer: Cabin baggage - it's usually a smaller dimension trolley or a bag which can conveniently be stowed in the hatracks or overhead compartment or under the seat in front of you. In most airlines it usually has a limit of being 7 or 8 KGS at the most. It's allowed in the cabin hence the name. Checked-in baggage - the suitcases and big bags which you literally have to check them in for the flight (example: you yourself checking into a hotel whereas in this case it's your bags in place of you n it's a flight In place of a hotel) and you receive a small baggage tag which corresponds to the baggage tag stuck on your suitcases n bags n has information about your final destination where you'll be receiving it after clearing immigration. Different airlines has varied rules and limitations for this one. In both cases if your baggage weighs more than the specified limit then you end up paying a heft sum for the excess weight.
